take: The market remains hostage to Strait of Hormuz dynamics, with a tanker hit by a drone over the weekend underscoring that the closure is not a clean, binary event, even as the US claims Middle East exports have rebounded to 15 million bpd against a pre-war average of 20 million bpd. This supply overhang is the single most critical driver for crude and products, as the threat premium persists despite the purported flow normalisation, keeping Brent and Dubai spreads elevated and refining margins volatile. In freight, the "detour economy" is the defining theme, with the Black Sea truce sought by Ukraine and the strike on Ust-Luga highlighting that war risk is stretching into the Baltic, which will keep tonne-mile demand and war risk premiums firm for tankers and bulkers alike. On flows, China's Q2 crude import drop confirms that higher prices from the disrupted Hormuz flows are already destroying marginal demand, whilst Asian buyers intensifying purchases of US crude as an alternative transit route points to a structural shift in arbitrage economics that will support the VLCC and suezmax market. Watch for any further UKMTO incident reports in the Strait over the next 24 hours, as a second successful drone strike on a commercial vessel would likely force a re-rating of the risk premium and send bunker prices in Singapore, which hit a four-month high in July, sharply higher.
